title: SeungYong Oh
text:
I am a veterinarian and Ph.D. student in the Laboratory of Developmental Biology and Genomics at the College of Veterinary Medicine, Seoul National University, working at the intersection of statistics and biomedicine. My current research focuses on analyzing single-nucleus RNA sequencing data from a mouse model of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
Methodologically, I am interested in statistical causal inference for biomedical data, particularly targeted learning and semiparametric inference. My long-term goal is to contribute to multi-modal data integration for precision medicine.

Definition 1 (Topology and Topological Space) A topological space is a pair \((S, \mathcal{T})\), where \(S\) is a set and \(\mathcal{T}\) is a collection of subsets of \(S\) (called open sets) satisfying:

\(\varnothing, S \in \mathcal{T}\),
any union of members of \(\mathcal{T}\) is in \(\mathcal{T}\),
any finite intersection of members of \(\mathcal{T}\) is in \(\mathcal{T}\).

We call \(\mathcal{T}\) a topology on \(S\). A set \(F \subset S\) is closed if \(S \setminus F \in \mathcal{T}\).


Definition 2 (Metric and Metric Spaces) A metric on a set \(S\) is a function \(d: S \times S \to [0, \infty)\) that satisfies

\(d(x_1, x_2) = 0\) if and only if \(x_1 = x_2\),
\(d(x_1, x_2) = d(x_2, x_1)\), and
\(d(x_1, x_3) \leq d(x_1, x_2) + d(x_2, x_3)\),

for \(x_1, x_2, x_3 \in S\). We call the pair \((S, d)\) a metric space.


Theorem 1 A metric space \((S,d)\) induces a topological space \((S, \mathcal{T}_d)\), where \[
\mathcal{T}_d \coloneqq \{E \subset S : E \text{ is open with respect to } d\}.
\]


Definition 3 (Openness and Closedness) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space with \(E \subset S\). Then \(E\) is said to be open if for every \(e \in E\), there exists an \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(\{x \in S: d(x, e) < \epsilon\} \subset E\). The subset \(E\) is closed if \(S \setminus E\) is open.


Remark. The definitions of openness or closedness in topological spaces are equivalent with ones in metric spaces.


Definition 4 (Closure) Let \(S\) be a topological space and \(A \subset S\). The closure \(\overline{A}\) of \(A\) is the intersection of all closed subsets of \(S\) containing \(A\), i.e., the smallest closed set containing \(A\).


Definition 5 (Interior) Let \(S\) be a topological space and \(A \subset S\). The interior \(A^\circ\) of \(A\) is the union of all open subsets of \(S\) contained in \(A\), i.e., the largest open set contained in \(A\).


Definition 6 (Boundary) Let \(S\) be a topological space and \(A \subset S\). The boundary \(\partial A\) of \(A\) is \[
\partial A = \overline A \setminus A^\circ.
\]


Definition 7 (Convergence) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. A sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset S\) converges to a limit \(x \in S\) if for any \(\epsilon > 0\) there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \[
d(x_n, x) < \epsilon, \quad \forall n \geq N.
\] It is denoted as \(x_n \to x\) (as \(n \to \infty\)).


Remark. In a metric space, a limit is unique.


Definition 8 (Cauchy Sequence) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. A sequence \(\{x_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset S\) is called a Cauchy sequence if for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exists \(N \in \mathbb{N}\) such that \[
\sup_{m, n \geq N} d(x_m, x_n) < \epsilon.
\]


Theorem 2 Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space, and let \(\{x_n\} \subset S\) be a sequence.

If \(\{x_n\}\) converges, then \(\{x_n\}\) is a Cauchy sequence.
If \(\{x_n\}\) is a Cauchy sequence and has a convergent subsequence, then \(\{x_n\}\) converges.



Definition 9 (Completeness) A metric space \((S, d)\) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in \(S\) converges to a point of \(S\). A subset \(E \subset S\) is complete if every Cauchy sequence in \(E\) converges to a point of \(E\).


Definition 10 (Open Cover) Let \(S\) be a topological space and \(E \subset S\). An open cover of \(E\) is a collection \(\{G_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in I}\) of open subsets of \(S\) such that \(E \subset \bigcup_{\alpha \in I} G_\alpha\). A subcover is a subcollection \(\{G_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in J}\), \(J \subset I\), which is still an open cover of \(E\).


Definition 11 (Compactness) A topological space \(S\) is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover. A subset \(E \subset S\) is compact if every open cover of \(E\) has a finite subcover.


Definition 12 (Lindelöf Space) A topological space \(S\) is called a Lindelöf space if every open cover has a countable subcover. A subset \(E \subset S\) is Lindelöf if every open cover of \(E\) has a countable subcover.


Definition 13 (Countable Set) A set \(A\) is countable if there exists an injective map \(f: A \to \mathbb{N}\). A set that is not countable is uncountable.


Definition 14 (Dense Set) Let \(S\) be a topological space. A subset \(A \subset S\) is dense in \(S\) if, for the closure \(\overline A\), \[
\overline A = S.
\]


Definition 15 (Separability) A topological space \(S\) is separable if it contains a countable dense subset. A subset \(E \subset S\) is separable if it contains a countable dense subset \(D \subset E\).


Theorem 3 Let \(S\) be a topological space. Then, the following hold.

If \(S\) is a compact space, then a closed subset \(E \subset S\) is compact.
If \(S\) is a Lindelöf space, then a closed subset \(E \subset S\) is Lindelöf.



Theorem 4 Let \(S\) be a metric space. Then, \(S\) is separable if and only if \(S\) is Lindelöf.


Definition 16 (Boundedness) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. A subset \(E \subset S\) is bounded if there exists \(r > 0\) such that \[
d(x, y) < r, \quad \forall x, y \in E.
\]


Definition 17 (Total Boundedness) Let \((S, d)\) be a metric space. A subset \(E \subset S\) is totally bounded if, for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there exist finitely many points \(x_1, \dots, x_n \in E\) such that \[
E \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^n B_\epsilon(x_i),
\] where \(B_\epsilon(x_i) = \{x \in S: d(x_i, x) < \epsilon\}\).


Theorem 5 Every totally bounded set is bounded. The converse is not necessarily true.


Definition 18 (Sequential Compactness) Let \(S\) be a topological space. A subset \(E \subset S\) is sequentially compact if every sequence in \(E\) has a convergent subsequence in \(E\).


Theorem 6 (Heine-Borel Theorem) For a set \(E\) in the Euclidean space \(\mathbb{R}^k\), the following are equivalent.

\(E\) is compact.
\(E\) is closed and bounded.



Theorem 7 (Generalized Heine-Borel Theorem) For a set \(E\) in a metric space \(S\), the following are equivalent.

\(E\) is compact.
\(E\) is sequentially compact.
\(E\) is complete and totally bounded.



Definition 19 (Polish Space) A Polish space is a topological space that is separable and metrizable in such a way that it becomes complete.


Remark. More explicitly, a topological space \((S, \mathcal{T})\) is called Polish if \((S,\mathcal{T})\) is separable and there exists a metric \(d\) on \(S\) such that \(\mathcal{T}\) is the topology induced by \(d\) and \((S, d)\) is complete.


References

Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill.

title: Influence Functions
Influence Functions
text:
Introduction
Let \((\mathcal{Z}, \mathcal{A}, P)\) be a probability space, and let \(Z\) be a random vector taking values in \(\mathcal{Z}\) with distribution \(P\). Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_n\) be i.i.d. copies of \(Z\). Suppose the density of \(Z\) belongs to the class \(\{p_Z(z; \theta): \theta \in \Theta\}\). Suppose the parameter \(\theta\) can be written as \(\theta = (\beta^\top, \eta^\top)^\top\), where \(\beta \in \mathbb{R}^q\) is the parameter of interest and \(\eta\) is the nuisance parameter that is finite- or infinite-dimensional. The true parameter is denoted by \(\theta_0 = (\beta_0^\top, \eta_0^\top)^\top\).
Consider the space \(\mathcal{H}\) of measurable functions \(\varphi: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}^q\) such that
\[
\mathcal{H} \coloneqq \{\varphi: \E_P[\varphi(Z)] = 0^{q \times 1}, \; \E_P[\varphi(Z)^\top \varphi(Z)] < \infty \},
\]
which is equipped with a covariance inner product \(\langle \varphi_1, \varphi_2 \rangle \coloneqq \E_P[\varphi_1^\top \varphi_2]\) and its induced norm \(\| \cdot \|\). We have shown that \(\mathcal{H}\) becomes a Hilbert space. (*) When there is no ambiguity, we write \(\E\) for \(\E_P\) and \(\E \varphi\) for \(\E [\varphi(Z)]\).
In this section, we consider finite-dimensional parametric models where
\[
\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb{R}^p,\quad
\beta\in\mathbb{R}^q,\quad
\eta\in\mathbb{R}^r,
\quad p=q+r.
\]
Most reasonable estimators \(\hat \beta_n\) for \(\beta\) are asymptotically linear, that is, they can be uniquely characterized by the influence function of the estimator.

Definition 1 (Asymptotically Linear) An estimator \(\hat \beta_n\) of \(\beta\) is said to be asymptotically linear if there exists a function \(\varphi \in \mathcal{H}\) (i.e., \(\E \varphi = 0\) and \(\E [\varphi^\top \varphi] < \infty\)) such that
\[
n^{1/2} (\hat \beta_n - \beta_0) = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(Z_i) + o_p(1),
\]
where \(o_p(1) \xrightarrow{p} 0\) as \(n \to \infty\). Here, \(\varphi\) is called the influence function of the estimator \(\hat \beta_n\).


Proposition 1 For an asymptotically linear estimator \(\hat \beta_n\) of \(\beta_0\) and its influence function \(\varphi \in \mathcal{H}\), it holds
\[
n^{1/2} (\hat \beta_n - \beta_0) \rightsquigarrow N \left(0, \E [\varphi \varphi^\top] \right).
\]


Proof. By the central limit theorem, it holds
\[
n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(Z_i) \rightsquigarrow N \left(0, \E [\varphi \varphi^\top] \right).
\]
Then, by Slutsky’s theorem, it follows \(n^{1/2} (\hat \beta_n - \beta_0) \rightsquigarrow N \left(0, \E [\varphi \varphi^\top] \right)\).


Example 1 Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_n \iid N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The maximum likelihood estimators for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) are given as
\[
\hat \mu_n = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i, \qquad \hat \sigma_n^2 = n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i - \hat \mu_n)^2.
\]
Then, we can write the expressions as
\[
n^{1/2} (\hat \mu_n - \mu_0) = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i - \mu_0),
\]
and
\[
n^{1/2} (\hat \sigma_n^2 - \sigma_0^2) = n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \{(Z_i  - \mu_0)^2 - \sigma_0^2\} - n^{1/2} (\hat \mu_n - \mu_0)^2.
\]
Since \(n^{1/2}(\hat \mu_n - \mu_0) = O_p(1)\) and \((\hat \mu_n - \mu_0) = o_p(1)\), \(n^{1/2} (\hat \mu_n - \mu_0)^2 = o_p(1)\). Therefore, both \(\hat \mu_n\) and \(\hat \sigma_n^2\) are asymptotically linear, and their influence functions are given as
\[
\varphi_1(Z_i) = (Z_i - \mu_0), \qquad \varphi_2(Z_i) = \{(Z_i  - \mu_0)^2 - \sigma_0^2\},
\]
respectively.


Theorem 1 An asymptotically linear estimator has a unique (a.s.) influence function.


Proof. Let \(\varphi, \varphi' \in \mathcal{H}\) be two influence functions of an estimator \(\hat \beta_n\). Then, it holds
\[
\begin{aligned}
n^{1/2} (\hat \beta_n - \beta) &= n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi(Z_i) + o_p(1), \\
n^{1/2} (\hat \beta_n - \beta) &= n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \varphi'(Z_i) + o_p(1),
\end{aligned}
\]
and thus
\[
n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \{\varphi(Z_i) - \varphi'(Z_i)\} = o_p(1).
\]
By the central limit theorem, \(n^{-1/2} \sum_{i=1}^n \{\varphi(Z_i) - \varphi'(Z_i)\} \rightsquigarrow N(0, \E[(\varphi - \varphi')(\varphi - \varphi')^\top])\). That is, \(\E[(\varphi - \varphi')(\varphi - \varphi')^\top] = 0^{q \times q}\) and thus \(\varphi = \varphi'\) a.s.


Example 2 (Super-efficiency and Hodges’ Estimator) Let \(Z_1, \dots, Z_n \iid N(\mu, 1)\), \(\mu \in \mathbb{R}\). The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of \(\mu\) is given by \(\bar Z_n \coloneqq n^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\), and we have
\[
n^{1/2} (\bar Z_n - \mu) \rightsquigarrow N(0, 1).
\]
Consider an estimator \(\hat \mu_n\) defined as
\[
\hat \mu_n = \begin{cases}
    \bar Z_n, & |\bar Z_n| > n^{-1/4} \\
    0, & |\bar Z_n| \leq n^{-1/4}
\end{cases}.
\]
When \(\mu \neq 0\),
\[
n^{1/2}(\hat \mu_n - \mu) \rightsquigarrow N(0, 1).
\]
When \(\mu = 0\),
\[
n^{1/2}(\hat \mu_n - \mu) \rightsquigarrow N(0, 0).
\]
Recall that the MLE is asymptotically efficient. That is, the MLE asymptotically achieves the Cramér–Rao lower bound, in this case, the variance \(1\) of \(N(0, 1)\). However, \(\hat \mu_n\) has a smaller variance than \(1\) when \(\mu = 0\). Such estimators are said to be super-efficient. Although they seem to be efficient, they have undesirable local properties (Tsiatis, 2006).


Definition 2 (Regularity) Consider a local data generating process (LDGP), where, for each \(n\), the data are distributed according to \(\theta_n\), where \(n^{1/2} (\theta_n - \theta^*)\) converges to a constant for some fixed parameter \(\theta^*\). That is,
\[
Z_{n1}, \dots, Z_{nn} \iid p(z, \theta_n),
\]
where
\[
\theta_n = (\beta_n^\top, \eta_n^\top)^\top, \quad \theta^* = ((\beta^*)^\top, (\eta^*)^\top)^\top.
\]
An estimator \(\hat \beta_n = \hat \beta_n(Z_{n1}, \dots, Z_{nn})\) is said to be regular if, for each \(\theta^*\), \(n^{1/2}(\hat \beta_n - \beta_n)\) has a limiting distribution that does not depend on the LDGP.


Remark. We only consider regular and asymptotically linear (RAL) estimators in what follows.
